# One api key is a standing service's whole credential story

Under mTLS peer auth, a service holding one narrowly-scoped api key enrolls at
startup, obtains its own certificate from the deployment CA, renews it without
the operator touching anything, and loses all access the moment that key is
revoked.

## Mint the service's key

`enroll-only.json`:

```json
{
  "name": "standing-service",
  "permissions": [{"action": "service:enroll"}]
}
```

```bash
rimsky auth create-key --endpoint "$BASE" --key "$ADMIN" \
  --name standing-service --role-file enroll-only.json

curl -sS --cacert ca.pem -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" \
  "$BASE/v1/auth/keys/standing-service"
# permissions: [{"action":"service:enroll"}]
```

That grant is the whole reach of the key:

```bash
svc() { curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' --cacert ca.pem \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $SVCKEY" "$@"; }

svc -X POST "$BASE/v1/enroll" -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"label":"probe"}'  # 200
svc "$BASE/v1/instances"                                                                   # 403
svc -X POST "$BASE/v1/auth/keys" -d '{"name":"x","permissions":[{"action":"*"}]}'           # 403
svc "$BASE/v1/audit"                                                                       # 403
```

## Start the service with that key and nothing else

```bash
docker run -d --network rimsky-net --network-alias standing -p 9400:9400 \
  -e RIMSKY_PEER_AUTH=mtls \
  -e RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_URL=https://rimsky-stack:8080 \
  -e RIMSKY_API_KEY="$SVCKEY" \
  -e RIMSKY_CONTROL_API_CA=/etc/rimsky/deployment-ca.pem \
  -v "$PWD/ca.pem:/etc/rimsky/deployment-ca.pem:ro" \
  <your service image>
```

Its api key, the control-API address, and the deployment CA root. No
certificate, no private key, no trust store written by hand.

## What the product does

The service comes up serving a certificate issued by `CN=rimsky-deployment-ca`,
whose subject is the id of the key it enrolled with. Its own listener refuses a
caller presenting no certificate.

Drive a node through that service and it settles fresh, so the credential the
service obtained at startup is the one carrying real work.

Inspect the serving certificate from outside with a client leaf from the
enrollment route:

```bash
curl -sS --cacert ca.pem -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" \
  -X POST "$BASE/v1/enroll" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{"label":"probe-client"}' > client.json
jq -r .cert_pem client.json > client.crt
jq -r .key_pem  client.json > client.key

openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:9400 -servername peer.rimsky.internal \
  -CAfile ca.pem -tls1_2 -cert client.crt -key client.key </dev/null
```

## Renewal needs no operator

A second enrollment on the same key returns a different certificate, and an
issued credential expires in about 23 hours — so it must be renewed to keep
working. Restart the service with nothing changed and it comes back serving a
credential from the same issuer.

The operator manages the key, not the certificates behind it.

## Revoking the key is the whole off switch

```bash
rimsky auth revoke standing-service --endpoint "$BASE" --key "$ADMIN"
```

The enrollment route answers the revoked key with an authentication failure
rather than a certificate, and a service restarted on that key exits fail-closed
rather than serving without credentials.
